cards.title: Lula wins election after final votes tallied

depth.text: Lula **won** Brazil’s election after the **final votes** were tallied
One commenter said Lula’s campaign **lit up** after a first-round setback, with Janones leading an online push that included a WhatsApp group called **“Lula’s army”** with 11 million people.

cards.camps: Two camps: some commenters welcome Lula’s win as a rejection of Bolsonaro; others say a fourth term gives one person too much power and is bad for democracy.

comments.text: I was seeing the reports from the first pass which said it was almost guaranteed that Lula would not win because of what the results of the first were. I wonder what caused that prediction to fail. I am glad the son of a failed coup organizer and a trump puppet didn't get elected and am hopeful for Brazils ability to self govern. Breaking free of US financial monopolies (credit cards) gives me…

This was the first time I saw a major mainstream media outlet prominently feature a statistical predictive model live during the vote count (and it was spot on): https://www.estadao.com.br/politica/eleicoes/em-tempo-real-p...

It was anyway a lose-lose situation. I hope to see Brazil free from 'bolsopetismo'/'bolsolulismo' (as some of we call this disease to keep Bolsonaro and Lula or their parties on the presidential room) soon, but here we go for another 4 years...
This is probably a good support case for run-off elections being beneficial.
As optimistic as I want to be, this is the fourth term for a president?? That cannot be good for democracy. It can be better than the alternatives and still not good.

cards.title: OpenAI and Anthropic cut their LLM prices by up to 80% within a few months. Why?

depth.text: OpenAI and Anthropic keep **cutting AI prices** as **open models** give them tougher competition
The timeline includes an **80% cut** to GPT-5.6 Luna. The author points to **open-weight competition** and **improved infrastructure** as possible reasons.
data: GPT-5.6 Luna input / output / cache-read price

cards.camps: Two camps: some credit competition and more efficient inference; others say limited demand or an unsustainable race to the bottom is driving prices.

comments.text: Competition drives prices down. We tried Kimi and GLM models after hitting 'cybersecurity' blocks on OpenAI and Anthropic. We found them to be much cheaper to access and helped us complete our work without 'cybersecurity' refusals blocking us.

DeepSeek claims $38 of revenue per GPU, per hour for Flash V4. That is $332,880 per GPU, per year. This matches their DeepInfer numbers: 25,600 output tokens/s per GPU sold at $0.60 per million -> $55 minus some other overhead to arrive at $38. For the bigger Anthropic and OpenAI models (and associated higher prices) there are many unknown factors. But presumably they also work hard on…

This is why Anthropic and OpenAI are pushing for more “regulation”. You can’t show ROI to investors by cutting inference costs. Regulation might inconvenience them a little, but the upside is huge if it means open models out of China get banned.
It’s a race to the bottom to see who blinks first and goes bankrupt. It’s not sustainable.

cards.title: AI use leads UC Berkeley math professor to see 'no point' in grading homework

depth.text: a Berkeley math professor stopped **grading homework** for correctness after students used AI to get **top scores**

**Richard Borcherds** now grades submitted homework for **completion**, not correctness, and says he has no alternative. He warned that if AI keeps improving at the present rate, human mathematicians may have nothing AI can't do better in a few years.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say AI makes homework easy to outsource and threatens learning; others say students still want to understand math and schools can change how they assess it.

comments.text: The irony here is perhaps missed by many. He didn’t grade homework in the first place. He paid assistants to grade. This is common practice among tenured professors with grant money to spend and graduate students beholden to them (I’m not making a moral statement, just noting this is common practice). Aside from the irony that Borcherds probably hasn’t graded a homework set in a while, instead…

As an aside, the professor in question is Richard Borcherds, fields medalist. He is probably most well known for proving the “Monstrous Moonshine” conjecture of Conway and Norton that there is some sort of correspondence between modular functions and representations of the Monster Group. When the conjecture was made in the 1970s, it was purely because someone noticed that a certain number was the…

This is quite sad. Even if students would cheat off each other, someone had to do the homework. And even the collaboration of cheating on homework always served as a forcing function for me or others to think about the material. If not actively, at least in the form of a quasi background radiation. With AI that is completely gone, and without reward loops for incremental work, the truth is there…

With some exceptions I think higher education should probably go back to being about academia and not necessarily teaching skills for industry. I think companies can now easily invest in their own extended training and grab people out of high school. Just a thought.

> Borcherds said he currently grades on completion if a student hands in their homework. In high school (2006) my physics teacher gave credit for handing in the homework (he checked it and handed it back, but no grade was assigned). Didn't hand in homework, you got a zero. He knew then that if you assign grades to hw, people will cheat. If I'm paying for Berkeley, the professor have office hours…

cards.title: JetBrains Thinkrail

depth.text: JetBrains built **ThinkRail**, an AI coding IDE that learns your project and keeps work **isolated**

ThinkRail wraps pi in a rich interface, with **separate git-worktree workspaces** and a **project spec graph** the agent maintains. It also has concurrent chats and comes as a **desktop app or CLI** that opens the same app in a browser.

cards.camps: Two camps: some think these IDEs just bundle tools people could use themselves; others are willing to give JetBrains a try.

comments.text: I refuse to take a repo with an AI-generated readme seriously. If you haven't bothered to write a readme, what else have you not bothered to do? (100% AI according to Pangram btw)

I’ve been using JetBrains IDEs for over a decade but rarely open them anymore because working on several worktrees concurrently is extremely frustrating and wasteful. Their AI strategy is all over the place and they always wanted to sell their opaque and overpriced tokens, which made no sense. I hope they get their act together.

Didn't JetBrains release JetBrains Air recently? This looks like it's basically the same basic premise, except implemented differently. What's their strategy here, are they just launching competing products? https://www.jetbrains.com/air/

It feels like JetBrains is dying, and they're trying very hard to survive. I liked their products. Also, personally I am not seeing next level devexp yet, other than just using my agents for everything

My take: I don't see the point of those new-IDEs. They are mostly just worktrees+sandbox+tabs+prompts, which is just git+docker+tmux+thinking, but if you actually learn to use those tools instead of handcuffing your agents to whatever take the IDE has, you're going to be much happier and effective. (That's also why there are so many of them: It just isn't that hard, everyone feels like a genius…

cards.title: Moderna and Merck say their mRNA cancer vaccine cut death, recurrence by 42%

depth.text: Moderna and Merck say a **personalized cancer vaccine** lowered melanoma patients’ **risk of death or recurrence**

In a Phase 3 trial of 1,137 patients whose melanoma had been surgically removed, adding intismeran to Keytruda lowered the risk of recurrence or death by **42 percent** after two years. **82 percent** of that group were alive without recurrence, versus **70 percent** with Keytruda and a placebo.
data: Risk reduction in recurrence or death
Risk reduction in distant metastasis or death

comments.text: Moderna's business model was always to be an on-demand vaccine platform, meaning a cost-effective service for ordering a few doses of a fully custom personalized vaccine. Their infrastructure looks more like a just-in-time 3D printer service than like a traditional vaccine development lab. It was a happy accident that the platform was available when we needed to come up with a COVID vaccine…

The Trump administration and RFK Jr. are actively working to prevent mRNA vaccines from reaching the market. People like Marc Andreessen, Larry Ellison and Elon Musk are actively supporting the administration, including hundreds of millions in donations to MAGA political campaigns in recent months. Should we hold these people accountable for the damage they're indirectly doing to public health?…

Amazingly, when this (IMHO quite good) data leaked, Moderna stock took a huge drop: https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article/moderna-sto ...
(Seems like people were expecting absolutely incredible, "cure for cancer" results and had already bid up the price a lot in advance.)
Related, if you are curious: this is what BioNTech is currently working on. https://www.biontech.com/int/en/home/pipeline-and-products/p...

So the absolute risk of recurrence/death on Keytruda alone was 30%, reduced to 18% with Keytruda plus intismeran. That will definitely make a noticeable difference in this disease if the real world results hold.

depth.text: one commenter tried a **new ordered map** and found it **slower in several workloads**

Swapping out std::BTreeMap made **union/difference +11% to +21% slower** and the **intersection stage +16% to +34% slower** in one 3D mesh test. A separate dictionary-words test found map<String, usize> used **40% more RAM** than std::collections::BtreeMap; commenters also questioned whether “fastest” holds across workloads.

glossary.run-off election: An extra election round where voters choose between candidates after an earlier round leaves no winner.
glossary.LLM: Large Language Model: an AI trained on lots of writing so it can take written questions and produce written answers.
glossary.open-weight model: A model whose trained settings are shared so other people can use them.
glossary.inference provider: A service that runs an AI model and sends its replies to an app.
glossary.cache read: Reusing saved text from earlier in a conversation instead of processing it all over again.
glossary.token: A chunk of text an AI reads or writes, often a whole word or part of one.
glossary.grading on completion: A teacher checks whether you turned the work in, rather than whether every answer is right.
glossary.AI agents: Computer programs that can carry out tasks, rather than only answer a question.
glossary.git worktree: A separate working copy of a project, so you can work on another task without mixing up files.
glossary.living specs: Project notes that describe what the software is meant to do and are updated as it changes.
glossary.CLI: Command-Line Interface: a way to control a computer by typing commands instead of clicking buttons.
glossary.MCP: Model Context Protocol: a standard way for AI apps to connect to outside tools.
glossary.pi: The coding agent ThinkRail runs to work on code.
glossary.mRNA: Messenger RNA: instructions that cells can use to make proteins.
glossary.Phase 3 trial: A later-stage test in people that compares a treatment with the usual care or another option.
glossary.intismeran: The name of the personalized mRNA vaccine used with Keytruda in this trial.
glossary.Keytruda: Merck’s cancer treatment used as the standard treatment in this trial.
glossary.placebo: A treatment with no active study drug, used so researchers can compare it with the drug being tested.
glossary.RFS: Recurrence-free survival: how long a patient goes without the cancer returning.
glossary.DMFS: Distant metastasis-free survival: how long a patient goes without the cancer returning in a different part of the body.
glossary.monoclonal antibody: A lab-made medicine designed to latch onto one particular target in the body.
glossary.BBS: Bulletin Board System: an online place people used to post messages and share files.
glossary.cracktro: A short intro that plays before a game, made by people who cracked its copy protection.
glossary.demo: A short computer-made display of visual effects, made to show what its creators can do.
glossary.demoscene: A community where people make computer demos to show off skill and creativity.
glossary.Hex View: A way to see a file's contents as numbers and change them.
glossary.Pascal: A programming language used in Denthor's tutorials.
glossary.ordered map: A collection that stores items in a chosen order and lets a program find one by its label.
glossary.B-tree: A way of keeping sorted items in a tree-shaped layout so a program can find them quickly.
glossary.trie: A way to organize words by their shared beginnings so software can find matching words quickly.
glossary.DRAM: Dynamic Random-Access Memory: the working memory a computer uses while running things.
